facts.statement: Chendytes was a goose-sized flightless marine duck that once lived along the California coast, the Channel Islands, and possibly southern Oregon.
facts.quote: Chendytes is a genus of extinct, goose-sized flightless marine duck, once common on the California coast, the California Channel Islands, and possibly southern Oregon.

facts.statement: Chendytes lived during the Pleistocene and survived into the Holocene, going extinct around 450–250 BCE.
facts.quote: It lived in the Pleistocene and survived into the Holocene. It appears to have gone extinct at about 450–250 BCE.

facts.statement: Humans exploited Chendytes lawi for at least 8,000 years, a duration unmatched by any other megafaunal genus in the North American archaeological record.
facts.quote: Archeological data from coastal California show a record of human exploitation of Chendytes lawi for at least 8,000 years.

facts.statement: Chendytes lawi specialized in eating sessile invertebrates and likely had a remarkable ability to wrench them off hard substrates.
facts.quote: Head and beak morphology suggest C. lawi ate invertebrates. Based on the large, robust morphology of the cervical vertebrae, skull, and bill, C. lawi specialized on sessile invertebrates and the species likely possessed "a remarkable ability to wrench off invertebrate animals attached to hard substrate".

facts.statement: Analysis of ancient DNA suggests Chendytes is a basal member of the tribe Anatini, representing a case of convergent evolution in feeding behavior rather than belonging to the tribe Mergini.
facts.quote: Although originally thought to be a seaduck in the tribe Mergini, analysis of ancient DNA sequences suggests that it is a basal member and a sister to the clade of extant dabbling ducks in the tribe Anatini, revealing an additional example of convergent evolution of characters related to feeding behavior among ducks.

facts.statement: The species Chendytes milleri was smaller than C. lawi and retained wings that had not degenerated as much.
facts.quote: C. milleri is smaller than C. lawi and the wings of C. milleri had not degenerated as much as those of C. lawi.

facts.statement: Fossil evidence of hundreds of bones and eggshells on San Miguel Island indicates the existence of nesting colonies, with one dated to approximately 12,000 radiocarbon years ago.
facts.quote: Hundreds of Chendytes bones and egg shells found in Pleistocene deposits on San Miguel Island have been interpreted as evidence that some of these island fossil localities were nesting colonies, one of which Guthrie dated to about 12,000 14C years (about 13,500–13,000 calibrated years B.P.).

facts.statement: Chendytes lawi was formerly classified within the subfamily Merginae.
The genus Chendytes existed from the Gelasian to the Holocene, spanning from 2.58 to 0 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Gelasian to Holocene (2.58 to 0 million years ago)
